title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is a chronic, immune-mediated orbitopathy most often associated with Graves disease. The condition arises from autoantibody-mediated inflammation targeting orbital fibroblasts, adipocytes, and extraocular muscles, resulting in a self-perpetuating cycle of cytokine release, tissue expansion, and fibrosis. Clinical manifestations include eyelid retraction, proptosis, diplopia, ocular surface disease, and, in severe cases, dysthyroid optic neuropathy. Disease activity varies from an early inflammatory phase to a stable inactive phase, with severity ranging from mild cosmetic changes to sight-threatening complications. Risk factors include smoking, thyroid dysfunction, age, sex, and genetic predisposition. Conservative measures such as lubrication and risk factor modification suffice for most cases. In contrast, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, targeted biologic therapy, radiotherapy, or surgical decompression are reserved for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease. Long-term outcomes depend on strict maintenance of euthyroid status, early recognition of disease activity, and timely referral for specialized management.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Through participation in this course, learners develop a structured understanding of TED pathophysiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, and evidence-based management strategies. The activity emphasizes early detection, accurate disease staging, and application of appropriate therapeutic interventions to improve visual and cosmetic outcomes. Participants learn to implement preventive strategies, interpret severity classifications, and apply multimodal treatment options across disease stages. Collaboration among an interprofessional team, including endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, oculoplastic surgeons, optometrists, pharmacists, and mental health professionals, enhances patient outcomes by aligning systemic and ocular care, addressing comorbidities, optimizing medication use, and supporting psychosocial health. Coordinated care ensures timely interventions for sight-threatening complications and facilitates long-term rehabilitation, enabling patients with TED to maintain visual function and quality of life.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Introduction
content: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammation of the orbit and is the most common cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults. [1] About 25% to 50% of Graves disease cases present with thyroid eye disease. [2] Goiter-associated ophthalmopathy was first described in AD 1000 by Avicenna and Al-Jurjani. In 1835, Robert Graves, an Irish physician, described 4 young women with thyrotoxicosis, palpitations, thyroid gland enlargement, and exophthalmos. Graves ophthalmopathy is an orbital inflammation or infiltration involving the periocular soft tissues, resulting in proptosis and ophthalmoplegia. [3]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Etiology
content: The etiology of TED is incompletely understood; this condition involves a complex, immune-mediated cycle involving the orbital fibroblasts, adipocytes, and lymphocytes. Marked orbital inflammation produces high levels of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1, and prostaglandins that target the orbital fat deposits. [4] Orbital fibroblasts are the primary drivers of the pathogenesis of TED because they have increased expression of thyroid-stimulating hormone receptors and can differentiate into mature adipocytes. [5] A subpopulation of orbital fibroblasts overexpresses the Thy-1 (CD90) marker. [6] Transforming growth factor-beta stimulates the Thy-1 fibroblasts to differentiate into adipocytes, while the Thy-1 (+) fibroblasts are stimulated to differentiate into myofibroblasts. [7] The thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor is the primary target of the autoimmune cascade within the orbit, and serum levels of thyrotropin receptor antibodies correlate with severity. [8] [9]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Etiology
content: Another possible target molecule is the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ, which is present on Thy-1(-) fibroblasts and regulates adipogenesis. [10] [11] The type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor is another critical autoantigen on Thy-1 (+) fibroblasts. [12] The stimulation of this receptor enhances the synthesis of IL-16 and the RANTES (regulated upon activation, normal T cell expressed and secreted) complex. This chemokine recruits CD4+ T cells in the orbital inflammatory cascade. [12] Thy-1 (-) fibroblasts activated by thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor activation differentiate into adipocytes, secrete IL-6, and recruit B cells and plasma cells. Thy-1 (+) fibroblasts, activated by the type 1 insulin-like growth factor, secrete IL-16 and RANTES to recruit T cells. T cells engage in CD40-CD154 interactions that induce IL-1 secretion from fibroblasts. [11]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Etiology
content: T cells also produce interferon-γ and tumor necrosis factor-alpha to stimulate myofibroblast activity and hyaluronate production. With IL-6 stimulation, B cells produce more autoantibodies within the orbit. With prolonged inflammation, the Thy-1 (+) cell cluster causes fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, leading to muscle-predominant orbitopathy. In contrast, TED cases with Thy-1 (+) cell clusters exhibit enlargement of the orbital adipose tissue, characterized by fat-predominant orbitopathy. Individuals younger than 40 have a higher Thy-1 (-) response and show orbital fat expansion. Individuals older than 70 are more likely to exhibit a Thy-1 (+) response, accompanied by fusiform muscle enlargement. [13]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of thyroid eye disease is approximately 50% among patients with Graves disease. The annual incidence is 16 per 100,000 women and 2.9 per 100,000 men in the United States. [2]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Epidemiology -- Risk Factors
content: Ethnicity : The prevalence is highest in Black individuals, followed by White and Asian persons. [14]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Epidemiology -- Risk Factors
content: Age : TED shows a bimodal incidence peak. The incidence is increased in women aged 40 to 44 and 60 to 64, as well as in men aged 45 to 49 and 65 to 69. [2] Older patients often have more severe disease and a higher chance of restrictive myopathy and dysthyroid optic neuropathy.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Pathophysiology
content: TED has a self-limited course owing to the absence of orbital lymphoid tissue. This absence prevents sustained immune activity, resulting in an active phase followed by a stable, quiescent phase. Wilson Rundle categorized the progression of TED into 3 phases, often referred to as the "Rundle Curve." Active or inflammatory phase: A steep rise in disease severity, lasting 6 months to 5 years (mean 2 years). Smoking can extend this stage. Static or plateau phase: Disease activity persists but does not progress. Inactive or burnout phase: TED usually improves after 18 months of disease activity. [22]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Pathophysiology
content: However, the disease rarely completely resolves, and residual fibrotic changes persist in the orbit. Aggressive immunosuppressive management during the initial active phase can limit the destructive and fibrotic consequences of the immune cascade. During the inactive phase, the disease does not respond to medical management and warrants surgical intervention. The cone model is divided into 3 phases and posits that disease progression is due to expansion of the muscle cone against a rigid bony orbit: Circumferential cone expansion displaces the extraconal fat outward, visible as fat prolapse into the upper and lower eyelids. Axial elongation of the cone displaces the globe forward, causing proptosis and muscle strain. Cone hypertension and muscle stiffness impede orbital venous drainage, manifesting as orbital venous congestion. [23]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- History and Physical
content: Ocular discomfort is the most common presentation in patients with thyroid eye disease. Other common symptoms are dryness, tearing, erythema, photophobia, and retro-orbital pain. Visual disturbances, such as blurring and diplopia, require prompt intervention. Furthermore, the onset of TED can precede the diagnosis of GD in 19.9% of cases. [24] Asymmetrical, bilateral TED is also a common presentation. Eyelid retraction is the most common clinical sign of TED, in up to 74% of cases.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- History and Physical -- Eyelid Changes
content: Lateral flare: The altered contour of the lateral upper eyelid is a pathognomonic sign caused by scarring between the lacrimal gland fascia and the levator aponeurosis. Eyelid lag: On a vertical downward pursuit, the excursion of the upper eyelid lags behind the globe. Lagophthalmos: Incomplete eyelid closure is a classic sign of TED. Lower eyelid retraction is present in up to 49% of TED cases. Upper eyelid retraction is present in around 90% to 98% of cases. The mechanisms proposed are as follows: Enlargement and fibrosis of the levator muscle are the most commonly affected muscles. Scarring between the levator aponeurosis and the surrounding soft tissues. Overextension of the levator muscle to counteract the ipsilateral tight inferior rectus muscle. Increased sympathetic stimulation of the Müller muscle. [9] [25]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- History and Physical -- Ocular Surface Changes (Active TED Phase)
content: Following inflammatory damage to the conjunctival mucous glands, the interface between the eyelid and the cornea is destabilized, resulting in tear film alterations. Lacrimal gland inflammation alters the tear film's protein profile and reduces the secretion rate. Persistent lagophthalmos disturbs the ocular surface, increases the reflex tear production rate, and alters the tear osmolarity. Dry eye symptoms and watering occur in 13% to 20% of patients. Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is observed in 0.9% of patients. Persistent dry eye with exposure keratopathy is observed in 1% to 8% of cases. [2] Corneal ulceration, perforation, and endophthalmitis are present in very severe cases. [26] Conjunctival chemosis is more common in moderate to severe cases and is seen in 15% to 25% of patients. [27]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- History and Physical -- Orbital Changes
content: Hypertrophy of the orbital fat and extraocular muscles within the bony orbit raises the intraorbital pressure. Forward protrusion of the orbit causes proptosis. Constriction of the superior ophthalmic vein by enlarged extraocular muscles results in venous stasis. Venous congestion causes redness and swelling of the eyelids, chemosis, and caruncular edema. [23] Dependent periorbital puffiness, often in the early morning, is also a sign of impaired venous outflow. Elevation of the episcleral venous pressure results in elevated intraocular pressure and open-angle glaucoma. [13] Venous and lymphatic stasis in the orbit prolongs the half-life of inflammatory cytokines, causing a cycle of inflammation. [13] Spontaneous fracture of the medial or inferior wall of the orbit resulting in spontaneous autodecompression. [28]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- History and Physical -- Extraocular Muscle Changes
content: Inflammation of the extraocular muscle (EOM) occurs during active TED. Infiltration of the EOM occurs through the accumulation of hyaluronate and the development of late-onset fibrosis. [29] The most commonly involved muscles are the inferior rectus, the medial rectus, the superior rectus, the lateral rectus, and the oblique muscles. [13] Restrictive strabismus and loss of binocular single vision. Diplopia presents initially in 6% to 18% of cases. Diplopia during the primary and inferior gaze is the most debilitating complication. [2] Fluctuation of diplopia is common, with worsening in the morning and during active disease. [29]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- History and Physical -- Optic Nerve Changes
content: Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON) is a potentially reversible optic nerve dysfunction in 4% to 10% of patients with TED [2] . Early symptoms include diminished vision, altered color vision, decreased contrast sensitivity, and constricted visual fields. See Table 1 . The possible mechanisms are: Compressive optic neuropathy: The most common cause is compression by the enlarged EOM at the orbital apex. [23] Optic nerve stretching: This occurs in cases of severe fat hypertrophy with proptosis. [30] Ischemic optic neuropathy: This occurs due to increased resistance to orbital arterial blood flow, leading to diminished perfusion. [31] Enlargement of the superior ophthalmic vein raises retrobulbar pressure and impairs tissue oxygenation. [31]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: Thyroid eye disease cases are clinically evaluated based on the disease activity and severity. The activity represents the grade of active inflammation and defines the progression of the disease. The severity reflects the spectrum of functional and cosmetic deficits. Numerous classification systems have emerged over the last century to assess and grade the clinical manifestations of TED.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: The most well-known system is the NO SPECS classification, which grades the clinical severity based on the mnemonic: No signs or symptoms, only (mild) signs, soft tissue involvement (eyelids and conjunctiva), proptosis, extraocular muscle involvement, corneal involvement, and sight loss (optic nerve injury). [32] The American Thyroid Association introduced this classification in 1969. It was updated in 1977 to the modified NO SPECS classification in which each letter was given a numeral 0 through VI. Each category was then subdivided into different levels of severity [33] . For example, the letter P, standing for proptosis in NO SPECS, was assigned grade III, with three subcategories assigned to different levels of proptosis as shown in Table 2 below.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: Notably, the NO SPECS system only grades the clinical severity of TED and does not assess the disease activity.  In 1981, Van Dyk proposed the RELIEF variation of the NO SPECS classification (see Table 3 ). [33] Because these classification systems dictate the treatment strategies without considering the status of active inflammation, they are now obsolete.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: A new system, the Clinical Activity Score (CAS), was proposed in 1989, considering the classic signs of inflammation, pain, swelling, redness, and impaired function (see Table 4 ). The European Group on Graves Orbitopathy (EUGOGO) later amended the CAS system. According to the amended CAS, active TED scores greater than 3 out of 7 points at the first visit or greater than 4 out of 10 points at subsequent visits. [34] The EUGOGO proposed a severity assessment protocol to categorize the severity of TED into mild, moderate-to-severe (see Table 5 ), and sight-threatening categories as summarized below:

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: A novel classification, the VISA system, was proposed in 2006 with four parameters: vision, inflammation/congestion, strabismus/motility restriction, and appearance/exposure. The International Thyroid Eye Disease Society defined separate parameters for the assessment at the first and subsequent visits in 2018. An inflammation (I) score greater than 4 of 10 points indicates inactive disease and should be managed conservatively. A score of greater than 5 out of 10 points with evidence of progression of inflammation should be managed aggressively. title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: Chemosis :+1 point if the conjunctiva lies behind the gray line of the eyelid, +2 points if the conjunctiva extends anterior to the gray line Eyelid edema :+1 point if no overhanging of tissues, +2 points if upper eyelid skin folds or lower eyelid festoons are present Strabismus/motility restriction : Ductions measured to the nearest 5° in all 4 gazes, using the corneal reflex method. Any change in the ductions of >12° in any direction suggests progression.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation
content: Clinical assessment protocols given by the VISA and EUGOGO teams are not interchangeable. Hence, only a single system should be used for a specific patient. All the scoring systems focus on a qualitative assessment, assigning equal weight to all symptoms, regardless of their diagnostic significance. The equality of symptoms could potentially undermine the accurate monitoring of disease progression. For example, the cut-off points (3/7 or 4/10 in CAS scoring) may not accurately reflect the extent of the disease.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation -- Ocular Imaging
content: Intraocular vasculature can be imaged using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA). OCTA analysis of the macula and the optic nerve head, which shows perfusion changes within the eye, corresponds to disease activity. [35] Choroidal imaging is also performed through enhanced depth imaging, high-definition optical coherence tomography, and swept-source optical coherence tomography of the subfoveal choroid. Subfoveal choroidal thickness changes are well-documented with progression of TED, with changes in the choroidal vascularity index corresponding to the severity. [36] The clinical role of these imaging modalities remains debatable, but early studies indicate a promising new trend in assessing intraocular vasculature in TED. Orbital Imaging Orbital imaging provides valuable insight into the diagnosis and management of TED.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography Scan
content: Characteristic fusiform enlargement of EOM is an enlarged muscle belly with relative sparing of tendons. Long-standing cases show significant EOM changes referred to as the "Coca-Cola bottle sign." Orbital imaging in unilateral TED cases confirms asymmetric bilateral EOM changes. [37] The Barrett index is useful for quantitatively measuring EOM thickness and apical crowding. [38] The vertical index is the sum of vertical muscle diameters divided by the height of the orbit. The horizontal index is calculated similarly. The greater of the 2 ratios is the Barrett index. A Barrett muscle index greater than 67% predicts optic neuropathy. [39]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography Scan
content: Imaging of dysthryoid optic neuropathy may show soft tissue signs like apical crowding, enlarged superior ophthalmic vein, enlarged EOM (especially the medial rectus), Barrett muscle index greater than 67%, orbital fat prolapse across the superior orbital fissure, perineural fat effacement, and enlarged lacrimal gland. The bony orbit signs may demonstrate an increased angle of the orbital apex and a greater angle of the medial wall. Coronal CT scan of orbital apex shows a narrow, clear ring of low density around the optic nerve due to bulging adipose tissue. Stretch neuropathy is diagnosed by a "taut nerve" in cases of severe proptosis. Classification of orbitopathy includes type 1 (lipogenic), type 2 (myogenic), and type 3 (mixed). Accurate coronal images aid in the detection of soft tissue remodeling of EOM and fat enlargement.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography Scan
content: CT exophthalmometry is the gold standard because it is accurate, reproducible, and unaffected by periorbital tissue edema. The interzygomatic line connects the ventral zygomatic borders bilaterally in axial view. The various techniques using the interzygomatic line are: The perpendicular distance between the anterior surface of the cornea and the interzygomatic line corresponds to the Hertel exophthalmometry value. [40] The distance between the interzygomatic line and the posterior sclera (normal value = 9.9 ± 1.9 mm). [41] The observation of less than one-third of the globe lying behind the interzygomatic line. [40] This technique is not feasible in patients who have undergone lateral wall decompression surgery. A novel method uses the posterior clinoid process as a landmark and measures the distance between it and the anterior corneal surface. [42]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation -- Magnetic Resonance Imaging Scan
content: MRI is an excellent modality for assessing disease activity. MRI parameters, such as the T2 signal-intensity ratio, the T1 signal-intensity ratio following gadolinium administration, and the apparent diffusion coefficient, correlate with the CAS severity scale. In T1-weighted images, the EOMs appear isointense to facial muscles in inactive TED, but enhance with gadolinium contrast. [43] In T2-weighted images, EOMs appear hyperintense during active TED and hypointense during inactive TED. [37]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Evaluation -- Orbital Color Doppler Imaging
content: This technique assesses the hemodynamic changes in the orbit following an increase in orbital volume. The primary vessels imaged are the ophthalmic artery, central retinal artery, and superior ophthalmic vein. The peak systolic velocity, end-diastolic velocity, and resistive index are important indicators of ocular perfusion. [44] TED demonstrates orbits with an initial increase in arterial blood flow during the inflammatory active phase, followed by a significant reduction in orbital blood flow during the inactive phase. [35] A sign of substantial loss in orbital arterial flow velocities occurs in vision-threatening TED and dysthyroid optic neuropathy. [35]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Prevention
content: Clinical assessment and accurate grading of thyroid eye disease are essential for appropriate management. Primary prevention includes smoking cessation. [45] Secondary prevention includes early detection of any dysthyroid state and prompt management to prevent disease progression; tertiary prevention includes using artificial tears to help prevent exposure keratopathy. [46] Cosmetic and visual rehabilitation are essential. Medical management includes the prompt restoration of euthyroid status, which is essential. [47]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Mild TED
content: Patients with corneal exposure and ocular surface symptoms require extensive lubrication with artificial tears, gels, and ointments. Overnight eyelid taping, occlusive eye pads, cold compresses, or sleeping with the head elevated are of questionable benefit. However, selenium supplements can improve the quality of life, reduce inflammation, and slow the progression of TED. [48] Eyelid retraction <2 mm is managed by: Transconjunctival injection: 5 units of botulinum toxin type A suspension Transconjunctival injection: 10 mg of triamcinolone suspension Both techniques demonstrate excellent results for the temporary resolution of eyelid retraction.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Active cases
content: Early immunosuppression is essential, and corticosteroids are the first-line treatment. The EUGOGO management protocol consists of low-dose pulse therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP), 500 mg weekly for the initial 6 weeks. Over the next 6 weeks, the dose is tapered to 250 mg weekly. [49] Severe active cases require prolonged oral corticosteroids for 6 months. Withdrawal of steroids may worsen the disease, but this can be prevented by adjuvant orbital radiotherapy. [50]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Active cases
content: Immunomodulators are considered  the second-line treatment. Indications for their use include steroid intolerance, steroid dependence, disease refractory to steroids, or contraindications to steroid use. Furthermore, methotrexate 7.5 to 10 mg weekly has shown a significant improvement in CAS and ocular motility within 12 months of treatment. [51] Azathioprine can be combined with low-dose orbital radiation or IVMP for moderate-to-severe TED [52] . Mycophenolate mofetil therapy demonstrated a superior CAS response with minimal disease reactivation compared to other treatment options. [53]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Immunobiologic agents
content: Rituximab, a humanized chimeric monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 on B cells, has shown a 100% response rate and minimal reactivation in patients with moderate-to-severe TED. [54] Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antibody), adalimumab (tumor necrosis factor[TNF]-α antibody), and infliximab (TNF-α antibody) also show promising results. Teprotumumab, a specific type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor blocker, is administered as 8 infusions over 24 weeks. The improvement in CAS, proptosis, diplopia, and quality of life, with a reduction in proptosis, is comparable to that achieved with surgical orbital decompression. [55]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Inactive cases
content: For cases with lagophthalmos, dry eye disease symptoms, and exposure keratopathy, adequate lubrication and corneal protection are advised. Appropriate surgical management is effective for residual proptosis, strabismus, eyelid retraction, and significant lagophthalmos. Surgical decompression in patients with euthyroid status and inactive disease provides sustained and predictable cosmetic results, with improvement in orbital perfusion. [56]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Sight-threatening disease
content: High-dose systemic corticosteroid, 1 g IVMP daily for 3 days, is the most effective therapy for DON cases. [57] Orbital radiotherapy is the second-line treatment that reduces the need for surgical orbital decompression. Urgent orbital decompression is reserved for active TED with DON, not responding to high-dose IVMP. [58]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical options
content: Elective surgical options are reserved for stable inactive thyroid eye disease cases not responding to conservative or maximal medical management. During cosmetic rehabilitation, orbital decompression surgery is the primary procedure to correct proptosis. After 6 months, strabismus surgery is performed to achieve adequate ocular alignment. After an additional 6 months, a definitive eyelid retraction surgery helps restore the cosmetic and functional status. Indications for orbital decompression are corneal exposure, DON, disfiguring proptosis, chronic pain or discomfort, and congestion. [59]

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Nonspecific orbital inflammatory disease: Bilateral proptosis with lacrimal gland enlargement EOM enlargement involves the muscle belly and the tendinous origin. The lacrimal gland enlarges and prolapses out of the lacrimal fossa. This disease can be associated with systemic autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, and IgG4-related disease. Serology and soft-tissue biopsy are diagnostic.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Prognosis
content: Approximately 80% of thyroid eye disease cases require conservative management with topical lubricant eye drops. [2] Approximately 5% of TED cases require systemic corticosteroids or immunomodulatory therapy. About 15% of patients undergo surgical intervention. Long-term follow-up and close monitoring for disease complications are essential.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Complications
content: Thyroid eye disease cases can present with the following complications: Dysthyroid optic neuropathy (compressive or ischemic) Optic atrophy Lagophthalmos, exposure keratopathy, or keratomalacia Open-angle glaucoma Restrictive strabismus with diplopia Persistent proptosis and eyelid retraction causing cosmetic disfigurement Orbital venous stasis and venous occlusion

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Cosmetic treatment is a crucial component of TED management. Common cosmetic concerns are proptosis, strabismus, upper and lower eyelid retraction, lateral flare, and lagophthalmos. Asymmetrical proptosis is common during inactive disease. A graded unilateral or bilateral surgical orbital decompression helps achieve a cosmetically symmetrical look. The surgical plan is customized based on the degree of proptosis correction, the pattern of strabismus, and the orbital anatomy.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Surgical orbital decompression corrects the proptosis by 2 to 2.5 mm per wall. [71] Orbital fat is the fifth wall of the orbit that can be used for surgical decompression. [69] Strabismus surgery is planned as a second-stage intervention, after the inflammation from the orbital surgery has subsided, and the tissue remodeling has stabilised. The restricted EOM is recessed to achieve orthophoria in primary gaze. The final correction for the eyelid retraction should be performed at least 3 to 6 months after the strabismus surgery. Blepharomyotomy, levator recession, and spacer grafts are common strategies for eyelid retraction correction.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Consultations
content: Patients with TED present to various care settings, from primary care to specialty clinics. These patients require thorough evaluation for ocular and orbital manifestations, thyroid status, and cardiovascular risk, with prompt initiation of thyroid hormonal treatment. TED management requires an interdisciplinary team that includes an ophthalmologist, an oculofacial plastic surgeon, an endocrinologist, an optometrist, a primary care clinician, and pharmacists. Timely referrals are crucial for optimizing visual and cosmetic outcomes.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: All patients with thyroid disorders should receive routine screening for early signs of thyroid eye disease. Regular follow-up of asymptomatic Graves disease and mild TED cases helps facilitate prompt diagnosis and management of sight-threatening complications. Clinicians should inform patients of the early signs of DON, which include altered color vision, diminished contrast sensitivity, visual field loss, and decreased visual acuity (loss of peripheral vision, as well as faded, dim, and blurred vision).

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Patients with classic symptoms of thyroid eye disease, but no history of thyroid disorders or who are euthyroid at presentation, require an endocrine evaluation and orbital imaging, which are essential for a definitive diagnosis in the absence of a typical clinical presentation. The management includes strict maintenance of euthyroid status, cessation of smoking, adequate lubrication, control of intraocular pressure, and monitoring of disease progression according to the CAS/VISA scoring systems at regular follow-up. Any sign of progression to active disease or sight-threatening disease warrants urgent management.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: TED cases require an interdisciplinary effort for early diagnosis and timely management. Clinicians and endocrinologists are the primary contacts for thyroid disorder cases. All predisposed patients should undergo regular eye evaluations. Long-term maintenance of euthyroid status is the foremost pillar for TED prevention. Smoking cessation and treatment of nicotine dependence are essential, with involvement of psychiatrists, addiction clinicians, counseling, and patient education. Sight-threatening disease and cosmetic disfigurement are also sources of anxiety for the patients. Mental health clinicians and social workers are essential for addressing psychosocial issues.

title: Thyroid Eye Disease -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Ophthalmologists and oculoplastic personnel are essential in the long-term follow-up, medical, and surgical management of TED cases. Visual and cosmetic rehabilitation are critical endpoints of TED management. Ophthalmologists and optometrists manage diplopia resulting from uncorrected or residual strabismus with prism correction, and ocular surface disease through various levels of dry eye therapy and surface protection (scleral lenses).
